title: Who by fire, who by water
hookLine: the High Holy Day prayer that ends: return, prayer and giving soften the decree

lines: ONE BY ONE, UNDER THE STAFF.
A LIST THAT STOPS THE BREATH.
cards: A shepherd stands at the gate of the fold, counting the flock. Each sheep passes under his staff, one at a time, and he looks at each one. That's the image at the heart of a prayer said on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Every living being passing, one by one, before God. And then the prayer starts listing what might happen to each of us this coming year. It's a list that makes a room go very still.
A singer once turned it into a well-known song called Who by Fire.

teach.b: Unetaneh tokef means let us declare the power, the power of the holiness of this day. It describes a heavenly court. A great shofar is sounded, and a still, small voice is heard.
Even the angels tremble. The book of memories is opened, and each person's signature is in it. Then the well-known lines.
On Rosh Hashanah it is written, and on Yom Kippur it is sealed. How many will pass away, and how many be born. Who will live, and who will die.
Who in their time, and who before their time.

teach.h: WHO BY FIRE, WHO BY WATER.
teach.b: Who by fire, and who by water. Who by sword, who by beast, who by hunger, who by thirst. Who will rest, and who will wander.
Who will be poor, and who will be rich. It's hard to hear, especially for anyone who has lost someone.
And then the whole congregation answers, often loudly, with the line the whole prayer turns on: but teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.
Return, prayer and righteous giving. They make the evil of the decree pass. Notice the wording.
Not they cancel the decree. They soften its evil, its harshness. People have read that many ways.
Some say these three can change what happens. Others say they change how we meet what happens. There's a medieval story that Rabbi Amnon of Mainz composed this prayer as he was dying, a martyr.
But texts found in the Cairo Geniza suggest the prayer is older than him. The story may be legend. The prayer is older than the legend.

how: Unetaneh Tokef is chanted in the repetition of the Musaf Amidah on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in Ashkenazi congregations, with the ark often open; the congregation says aloud the closing line about teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.

o: the prayer of who by fire, who by water
the last prayer that closes Yom Kippur
the shofar blessing said on Rosh Hashanah

games.q: the list ends: who by fire, who by water, who will be poor, who rich. what does the congregation answer?
o: but return, prayer and giving make the evil of the decree pass.
games.why: teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah: they don't erase the decree, but they soften its harshness.

practice: Hold each of the three in mind for a few breaths: teshuvah, returning to a better way; tefillah, prayer, or simply honest words; tzedakah, giving to someone who needs it.
Notice which one is calling you today, an apology, a few honest words, a gift, and let it settle.
